title: Customer workload taxonomy for dedicated capacity negotiation
creator: Maya Singh
description: Create a repeatable workload taxonomy and negotiation guidance that maps customer signals to recommended SLA targets, reserved throughput levels, GPU class suggestions, and scaling policy templates. Outcomes: faster intake decisions, consistent negotiation language for sales/solutions, and a data-forward recommendation to engineering for pool sizing and fallback rules.
background: Customers repeatedly bring heterogeneous throughput and latency SLAs during dedicated capacity conversations. Currently our intake is ad-hoc: sales and solutions engineers estimate needs manually and engineering runs sizing exercises. This leads to long cycles, overprovisioning, and inconsistent contract terms. Several past onboarding cases (Q3–Q4 2025) highlighted re-negotiation due to mismatched burst behavior and missing instrumentation for actual token patterns.
goals: (1) Define a compact workload taxonomy capturing steady-state qps, burst profile, percentiles (p50/p95/p99 latency), request length distribution, KV/prefix cache hit-rate sensitivity, and sync vs async traffic. (2) Produce a deterministic mapping from taxonomy bucket to recommended reserved throughput, GPU family, and scaling policy. (3) Create templated negotiation language and contract clauses that standardize burst credits, pre-warming windows, and prioritized fallbacks.
scope: Customer requests intake -> taxonomy classification -> recommendation artifact consumed by Sales/SE/Concord. Includes sample scoring rubric, required telemetry fields, and a negotiation cheat-sheet. Does NOT include implementing autoscaling code paths or runtime allocation automation (that will be separate ENG work).
out_of_scope: Code changes to allocator, billing engine updates, and legal contract drafting. Implementation of instrumentation ingestion outside of the minimal telemetry checklist.
success_metrics: 1) Time from intake to first sizing recommendation <= 48 hours for 90% of enterprise leads. 2) Reduction in initial overprovisioning (measured as committed vs. actual consumed reserved GPU hours) by >= 20% after rollout. 3) Decrease in SLA re-negotiations within 90 days by >= 30%.
proposed_solution: Deliver artifacts in three parts: 1) Workload Taxonomy (4 buckets: latency-tiered, throughput-bounded, burst-dominant, cache-sensitive) with definitions and observable thresholds. 2) Mapping matrix: For each bucket, output a recommended reserved throughput (tokens/sec or reqs/sec), GPU class guidance (e.g., A100-40GB vs H100-80GB vs inference-tuned T4 equivalent), and scaling policy template (min/max nodes, burst credit allowance, pre-warm time). 3) Negotiation Kit: a one-page rubric for Sales/SE with example phrasing, SLO examples, and an FAQ addressing common customer requests (bursting, region preferences, failover to hosted).
workload_scorecard: Scoring rubric (example): 1) Throughput score = log10(steady_tokens_per_sec + 1) scaled to 0-10. 2) Burst score = peak_multiplier * (burst_duration_hours / 1hr) scaled to 0-10. 3) Latency sensitivity = p95_target_ms < 200 -> +2, < 100 -> +4. 4) Request length penalty: avg_tokens > 1024 -> +2 to GPU-class needs. Combine weighted sum (weights: throughput 0.45, burst 0.25, latency 0.2, cache-sensitivity 0.1) to place into taxonomy bucket. Output recommended reserve by converting throughput score to reserved GPU equivalents using historical throughput-per-GPU curves (engineering will validate).
negotiation_guidelines: 1) Frame burst credits as a finite, measurable resource: offer X burst credits per month tied to percent of committed throughput. 2) Use pre-warm windows: for predictable traffic spikes, require 15–60 min pre-warm to achieve lower latency SLAs. 3) Fallback tiers: standard contract includes graceful fallback to narrower model family with explicit latency delta and optional compensation terms. 4) Billing: recommend committing on reserved throughput in tokens/hour with a provision for auto-convert to pay-as-you-go for transient bursts above threshold. 5) Example phrasing: 'We recommend committed throughput of <value> tokens/sec with <Y> burst credits/month. For sustained usage above commit, charges will be applied at the burst rate unless a higher committed band is purchased.'
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (2 weeks): Draft taxonomy and rubric; validate against 10 recent enterprise intakes. Phase 2 (3 weeks): Build an intake form for Sales/SE and publish the Negotiation Kit; run 3 shadow intakes. Phase 3 (4 weeks): Integrate rubric into the onboarding checklist; collect telemetry from first 10 customers and refine mapping. Handoff ENG backlog items (allocator sizing tasks) as dependencies for automation in Q2.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Customers may under-report burst patterns leading to SLA miss. Mitigation: require historical request traces for 30-day period or accept conservative default multiplier; include rollback clause. Risk: Mapping may under/over recommend GPU class. Mitigation: label recommendations as 'initial guidance' and include explicit handshake with ENG sizing review within first 14 days of onboarding. Risk: Sales wants looser language for faster closes. Mitigation: provide a two-line summary and mandatory checkbox that acknowledges the recommendation is based on provided signals.
next_steps: Schedule kickoff with Sales/SE and ENG (1-week)
Pilot taxonomy on three pending enterprise RFPs (2-week)
Create Sales intake form in Notion and collect sample telemetry fields (1-week)
Draft Negotiation Kit and get Legal review (2-week)
Create ENG ticket(s) for allocator verification and per-GPU throughput curves (depends: ENG-78112)
